19764-the-moccasin-ranch-a-story-of-dako:
Hamlin Garland called The Moccasin Ranch a story of Dakota, and dated it 1909. Its Dakota is cold, wet, and hard: ice-ridged fields, swales full of water. Geese fight the wind overhead while ducks sit on ice-rimmed ponds. The sod lies burned black and bare, firm with frost. A wagon rattles noisily over that frozen ground.

Garland built his name on honest tales of farm hardship. He rejected pretty lies about pioneer life. Dakota settlers in his work face debt, weather, and loneliness. The ranch of the title concentrates those pressures. Readers get realism from a man who lived the life. This tale is Garland in his true country.
19932-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Slave Narratives gathers first-person accounts of American slavery, a folk history in the tellers' own words. One woman remembers a morning her mother was gone. She woke, went to her mother's room, and found her missing. She cried and cried for her, she says. Her mistress would not let her leave the house to search. The fear was she would try to find her mother. Such separations haunt narrative after narrative here.

The Federal Writers' Project interviewed elderly survivors in the 1930s. Their dialect was written down as spoken, however imperfectly. Thousands of pages record work, family, faith, and cruelty. No other source lets the enslaved describe slavery so fully. These volumes anchor American memory of the institution. Every page is testimony, not literature alone.
20222-an-ethical-problem-or-sidelights-u:
An Ethical Problem weighs experiments on men and animals in science. Its subtitle calls it sidelights upon such work, pro and con. Public feeling on vivisection is confused, the book says at once. No agreed definition of the word itself has yet been fixed.

That lack of a shared term muddles every debate on the subject. The book sets out phases of animal experiment one by one. It asks where knowledge ends and cruelty begins in the lab. Readers get a sober, early map of a fight that still runs hot today.
20524-culm-rock-the-story-of-a-year-what:
Glance Gaylord's Culm Rock tells the story of a year in a boy's life on a barren shore. Culm Rock is a point of rock and sand where the sea is never silent. It would have been an island but for narrow strips of sand heaped high like ridges.

That slender bridge binds the rock to the mainland. Often it seems the hungry sea will tear the bridge away. In that lonely place, the year brings the boy loss, work, and faith. The story belongs to the religious tales once given to children as Sunday reading.
20785-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
A man born in Louisiana ten years before the Civil War tells his tale in his own words. He recalls the war's start with a child's clear memory. His voice is one of many in Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States.

In the 1930s, field workers wrote down the memories of the last living ex-slaves. Work, food, faith, cruelty, and freedom fill their plain, strong talk. These accounts form a key source for American history, told from below. No reader can meet these voices and keep a thin view of the slave past.
21268-the-search-for-the-silver-city-a-t:
James Otis set this tale of adventure in Yucatan, published in New York in 1893. The region was then almost as unknown as the interior of Africa. His introduction quotes E. G. Squier on the blank map between Chiapas, Tabasco, Yucatan, and Guatemala, where the Usumacinta River gathers a thousand tributaries. Maya peoples who resisted Spain still sheltered there.

Young Neal, pictured wrestling a great reptile, joins the search for a fabled silver city in that fastness. Jungles, plains, pine plateaus, and hidden ruins fill the road. Otis wrote many boys' adventure books, and this one mixes real Central American geography with a treasure hunt.
21508-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Former slaves tell their own lives in the South Carolina narratives, part two, gathered in the late 1930s. Federal Writers' Project staff typed the interviews from 1936 to 1938. The Library of Congress issued the set in 1941 as a folk history of slavery.

One woman tells how her mother was free before the war, so she herself was never enslaved. Others recall farm work, town hotels, masters, and kin lost or kept. The editors kept each speaker's own spelling and turns of phrase. These plain voices form a record no outside history could supply, and they demand slow, heedful reading.
21640-a-bid-for-fortune-or-dr-nikola-s-v:
Guy Boothby's Dr Nikola returns in A Bid for Fortune, or Dr Nikola's Vendetta, reissued in 1918. A restaurant manager on the Thames Embankment opens the prologue in a state of dread. Nikola's letter and a fine repeater watch, at half-past seven, mark the hour of crisis.

The narrator's holiday in Sydney turns into a chase through London and Port Said. Imprisonment, escape, and a free passage granted by Nikola himself follow. Lord Beckenham's tale and a trail through the islands close the hunt. Boothby's master villain, cool and ruthless, made the Nikola tales a sensation of their day.
21764-child-stories-from-the-masters-bei:
Great poems and works of art become simple tales for children in Maud Menefee's Child Stories from the Masters. The book appeared at the turn of the century. Menefee had told stories to the same circle of children for years, and drew on the great books when she needed fresh material. She does not retell full plots, which lie beyond a child's reach. Instead she takes a scene, a stanza, or a single purpose from each work.

Pippa passes into spinning and weaving games, while Siegfried and Parsifal arrive as knight tales with their music. Millet's Spinner fronts the book. Menefee hoped teachers would use her method with their own classes. She wanted children brought close to poetry and art early, through story and handwork together.
21781-text-book-of-biology-part-1-verteb:
Backboned animals are the subject of this textbook of biology, part one of two, devoted to the vertebrates. The book was later reworked by A. M. Davies in 1898 as a textbook of zoology, then revised again by J. T. Cunningham. This text keeps the first and second editions, with dissections redrawn by Miss A. Robbins. It was built for students learning animal structure at the bench.

Chapters teach through dissection, with labeled plates and careful terms for each part. The transcriber fitted the text for voice readers, hoping blind students and children could use it too. As a period schoolbook, it shows how biology was taught when the knife and the drawing, not the screen, trained the eye.
22166-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
In the 1930s the Federal Writers' Project sent interviewers across the South to record former slaves. Their typescripts, assembled by the Library of Congress, form the Slave Narratives. This volume holds life stories told in the speakers' own words. Elisha, an old man, tells his interviewer he foresaw her coming to write down his memories.

Narrators recall sale, labour, hunger, kindness, cruelty, and freedom's arrival. Their speech is kept in dialect spelling, which modern readers handle with care. Taken together, the interviews are the largest body of testimony from the enslaved themselves. Historians lean on them heavily. Few books in this library carry voices of such direct witness to slavery.
22976-slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of:
Louisa Adams introduces herself in these Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States. My name is Louisa Adams, she says. I was born in Rockingham, Richmond County, North Carolina, and was eight years old when the Yankees came through. She belonged to Master Tom, her mother was Easter, her father Jacob, and she names her brothers and sisters in order.

Thousands of such interviews were gathered in the 1930s from the last living Americans born enslaved. Work, family, punishment, food, and freedom fill their pages in the speakers' own words. No history of slavery carries their weight of witness. The dialect spellings belong to the interviewers' practice of the time, and readers should hear the voices through them, not past them.
a-bid-for-fortune-or-dr-nikola-s-vendett:
A Bid for Fortune, or Dr Nikola's Vendetta, is an 1895 thriller by Guy Boothby, and the book that introduced Dr Nikola. Nikola may be the world's first modern supervillain: a master of hypnotism and mind control, a telepathic adept, and a skilled astral projectionist. He can make ordinary men see images in pools of liquid and can prophesy the future, and it is said he knows the hour and manner of his own death.

Against such a villain, Boothby sets a tale of pursuit and vendetta in the sensation style of the 1890s. Nikola's calm, occult power made him unlike the criminals of earlier fiction, and he returned in later Boothby novels. The book stands at the head of that series, where the supervillain first steps forward.
a-cumberland-vendetta:
John Fox Jr. opens in a cave above a Kentucky river, where a tall mountaineer and a boy with a squirrel rifle longer than himself step out into the rhododendrons. The cave was their childhood hiding place and stays their refuge when hunting. Below them lies a valley divided by an old feud between two families.

The tale follows the vendetta's code: ambush, reprisal, and young love growing across the line between the houses. Fox, who knew the Cumberland country well, writes the mountains, the cornfields on steep slopes, and the people's speech with a local's ear. His feud story became a small classic of Appalachian fiction, sadder than it is violent.
a-monk-of-cruta:
A Monk of Cruta is an 1894 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, written early in his long career. Oppenheim later became one of the best-known English thriller writers of his time, but this book dates from before that fame. It survives as one of his earliest works of fiction, from the period when he was still finding his ground as a novelist.

Modern reprints present it as a fascinating novel of its period, and it is now scarce in early editions. For readers, its interest lies in seeing the young Oppenheim at work before the spy stories and international intrigues that made his name. The book preserves the starting point of a major popular career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-grot: This article covers Grottaferrata, the Greek-rite abbey by Rome. St. Nilus founded it a thousand years ago. Douglas Raymund Webster honors its Eastern ways. East and West meet in its choir. Its monks still chant in Greek on feast days.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andres-urdane: A 1913 entry on Andrés Urdaneta — the Augustinian who found the Pacific way home. Camillus Crivelli honors his navigation. His tornaviaje saved the Manila trade. The friar who mapped the ocean. Spain's sailing monk. His charts guided the galleons home.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-biretta: A 1913 entry on the biretta — the cleric's square cap. Herbert Thurston traces its academic roots. The three wings crown the doctor. The priest doffs it at the altar. The headgear of the learned clergy. Its tassel marks the doctor's rank.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-della: A 1913 entry on Della Porta — the Roman architect. Gerhard Gietmann honors his famous dome. He crowned St. Peter's mighty cupola. The city prized the master hand. The Michelangelo's great successor. His 1602 death is famed. His Villa Aldobrandini is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gines-perez-d: A 1913 entry on Pérez de Hita — the Murcian writer. Ventura Fuentes honors his famous Guerras. His pen sang the Granadan wars. Spain prized the vivid tales. The Froissart of the Moorish wars. His 1619 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-giud: This 1913 reference piece on Giona Battista — the convert scholar. Francis X.E. Albert notes his famous works. The entry preserves his modest fame. His pen served the seventeenth century. A writer among the converts. His 1668 works are famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-house-of-mala: This 1913 reference article on the Malatesta — Rimini's lords. Edmund Gardner unfolds their famous rule. They held the Romagna's towns. The poets sang the tragic house. The signori of the Adriatic shore. Their 15th-century rule is famed.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moneta: Moneta was an ancient city important enough to host a Christian bishop in the early centuries, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its church history. A quiet name from the ancient map.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-monita-secret: The Monita Secreta purported to reveal the Jesuits' secret instructions for seizing power, but it was a forgery, probably by a disgruntled ex-Jesuit. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mozzetta: The mozzetta is the short cape worn by popes, cardinals, and bishops, its color marking rank. This entry explains its forms, its history, and who may wear it. Authority, shouldered: its red, purple, and white versions mark pope, cardinal, and bishop.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystical-stig: The stigmata are the wounds of Christ reproduced in the bodies of saints, from Francis of Assisi onward. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-north-dakota: North Dakota's Catholic story runs from the missionaries of the Red River to the dioceses of Fargo and Bismarck. This entry covers its bishops, parishes, and institutions. The faith on the northern plains: its parishes followed the wheat and the railroads.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-paruta: Paolo Paruta was the Venetian statesman-historian whose histories defended the republic's liberty. This entry covers his career, his works, and his thought. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-regesta: The papal regesta are the great registers preserving the popes' letters across the centuries. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-of-samos: Paul of Samosata was the heretical bishop of Antioch deposed for denying Christ's divinity. This entry explains his doctrine, his trial, and his condemnation. The bishop who fell from the faith: his solemn deposition freed ancient Antioch at long last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pforta: Pforta was the famous Saxon school whose alumni shaped German letters. This entry covers its foundation as a Cistercian abbey, its transformation, and its scholars. catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-augusta: Port Augusta became the diocese of South Australia's far north. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and institutions as of 1913. The faith at the desert's gate: its humble cathedral serves the vast red outback of South Australia's far north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raccolta: The Raccolta is the Church's book of indulgenced prayers. This entry explains its origin, its contents, and its use. The treasury of the faithful's prayers: its worn pages grant the precious indulgences of Rome's rich treasury of grace and mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sabrata: Sabrata, the Libyan port of the Tripolitanian coast, once had a Christian bishop. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from Tripolitania: its Roman theater crowns the shore of Libya's coast in the sun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sacra-romana-: The Sacra Romana Rota is the pope's supreme tribunal. This entry explains its judges, its cases, and its procedure. The wheel of the Roman justice: its learned auditors judge the causes in Rome's palace of justice today still in session.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salta: Salta became the diocese of Argentina's northwest. This entry covers its bishops, its cathedral, and its history. The faith of the Andean valleys: its pink cathedral crowns Salta in Argentina's northwest in the Andes' foothills of the province's capital city.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saskatchewan-: Saskatchewan and Alberta became the vicariate of the prairie missions. This entry covers its Oblates, its stations, and its history as of 1913. The faith of the Canadian northwest: its Oblate missions dot the prairies in the 1860s' decades of the west.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-serafino-porr: Serafino Porrecta was the Dominican theologian of Naples. This entry notes his Summa, his teaching, and his fame. The master of the Neapolitan schools: his learned Summa crowned Naples in the 1570s' schools in the city of the Dominicans in the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-south-dakota: South Dakota became the state of the Black Hills. This entry covers its history, its church, and its people as of 1913. The Catholics of the prairie dioceses: their many churches dot the state in the 1900s' dioceses in the plains.

catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eusebius-o: St. Eusebius of Samosata was the martyr bishop. This entry traces his see, his Arians, and his crown. The confessor of the Eastern church: his ancient see crowned Samosata in the 360s' Euphrates in the east of the empire in Commagene.

dutt-manu-samhita:
Dutt's English Manu Samhita appeared in 1909, late in his translating career. The Laws of Manu form ancient India's great code of duty. No legal text has shaped Hindu custom more deeply over time.

The code sets out caste duties, marriage, food, and rules for kings. Penance, gifts, and the stages of life get the same firm order. It also teaches the soul's path through duty toward final release. Scholars use the text to grasp classical India's social frame. Dutt's version keeps the famed code open to plain English readers today. Its rules, harsh and humane by turns, reward careful, critical reading.
essays-before-a-sonata: Charles Ives's Essays Before a Sonata meditates on music and thought. The great composer ponders Thoreau, Emerson, and the American spirit. Deep philosophy and high art intertwine throughout. A bold and unique American mind on the page.
europe-and-the-faith-sine-auctoritate-nu: Europe and the Faith, Sine Auctoritate Nulla Vita, Hilaire Belloc's Catholic history. The faith's Europe. This book preserves that history. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
gjellerup-der-pilger-kamanita:
Karl Gjellerup set his novel of ancient India in the days of the Buddha, and German readers meet it here as Der Pilger Kamanita. Kamanita, a merchant's son, leaves wealth and comfort behind. His road leads toward a teaching that promises release from pain and desire.

Along the way, love, loss, and chance meetings test the young pilgrim's resolve. Gjellerup, who shared the Nobel Prize in 1917, writes with calm and grace. East and West meet in the tale, since a Danish author retells an Indian quest. Readers find a serene story of the search for truth and inner peace.
govdocs-archive_org-mda-mdma-and-other-m:
Torsten Passie and Udo Benzenhöfer, historians of medicine, wrote this study of MDA, MDMA, and related mescaline-like substances in the American military's search for a truth drug. Their period runs from the 1940s to the 1960s, the Cold War decades of secret drug research.

Drawing on the documentary record, they trace how military and intelligence researchers tested these compounds on people, hoping for a substance that would loosen tongues in interrogation. MDMA appears in the files decades before it became a street drug, and later a therapy candidate. The paper is a documented chapter of psychopharmacology's secret history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-LorenzMarita_Lo:
Vanity Fair published 'The Spy Who Loved Castro' in November 1993, a profile of Marita Lorenz. Lorenz had been a lover of Fidel Castro as a young woman. She later claimed knowledge of plots around the Kennedy assassination, and her story pulled her into that debate for decades.

The profile appeared thirty years after Dallas, when magazines were revisiting the case for the anniversary. Lorenz's life crossed the era's main currents: Castro's Cuba, exile politics, intelligence work, and courtroom testimony. The piece presents her as she presented herself, a woman who said she had stood close to famous events. Readers can weigh her claims against the record she never quite settled.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MilitaryAssista: The Department of State Bulletin reprinted this statement by Secretary of State Dean Rusk under the title 'International Defense Commitments of the United States.' Rusk set out the treaties and pledges that bound the United States to defend other countries. Statements of this kind were the government's public map of its Cold War obligations. The file preserves the reprint under a military-assistance heading, without a date or further detail.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MusgroveRita_Mu:
A writer signing himself 'Fred' sent this letter to 'Ed' on July 8, 1974. The two men were exchanging assassination literature among the critics of the official account. Fred mentions William Turner's piece in Ramparts magazine. He also encloses a column by Mike Royko, the Chicago columnist.

At the letter's end, Fred states his own conclusion: President Kennedy's life was taken by a small conspiracy. The letter is a sample of how the research community actually worked. Books and articles moved by mail between men who mostly knew each other by post. Along with the clippings went judgments, argued in the margins, like the one this letter closes with.
govdocs-archive_org-strike-of-the-russia: The Strike of the Russian Gods attacks world religions from a pagan point of view. It also charges those religions with mind control over their followers. The library holds the book as an archive item, without backing, and classes it as fringe material. Its value for study lies in its stance: a modern pagan writer turning the language of exposure against the faiths that replaced his own gods.
la-fiammetta:
Giovanni Boccaccio wrote La Fiammetta, translated here by James C. Brogan in 1907. Its prologue calls it the elegy of Madonna Fiammetta. She sends her tale to ladies in love.

Fiammetta speaks in her own voice about her sorrows in love. She hopes her pain will win pity from happier women. She does not want her words to reach the ears of men. The book stands as an early, intense portrait of a woman abandoned by her lover. Her grief unfolds as a long, direct address to women readers. Few early books give a woman's sorrow this much space.
lucasta:
Lucasta gathers the poems of Richard Lovelace, the Cavalier poet. The first part holds poems addressed to Lucasta herself. Songs tell of going beyond the seas and going to the wars. There are odes to a rose, a dialogue, and Lucasta weeping.

One famous piece is 'To Lucasta, from Prison,' an epode of defiance. Lovelace fought for King Charles in the Civil War and knew prison. His verses mix love, honor, and a soldier's swagger. 'Stone walls do not a prison make' is his best-known boast. Lucasta herself was the lady who inspired his finest songs. The poems shine with the grace of the Cavalier age.
mary-gusta:
Joseph C. Lincoln set Mary-'Gusta in the Cape Cod town of Ostable. Talk fills the town on the day Marcellus Hall is buried. Folks ask what will become of the child Mary-'Gusta now.

Marcellus had lived in Ostable for fifty nine years, much talked of. The girl had drawn scant thought while he lived. Lincoln opens with a young news man at work on the death notice, and with a town keen to guess. Even the death notice shows Lincoln's dry Cape Cod humor. Big questions in town start, here, from one small girl's fate.
nasa-tm-19630006262-the-effects-of-wing-:
Stuart L. Treon of Ames Research Center wrote this NASA memorandum, TM X-364, in April 1960. It asks how wing shape affects a flat-top hypersonic aircraft. Plan form means the wing's outline as seen from above. Tests ran from Mach 0.6 to 1.4, through the sound barrier.

Treon measured pitch stability traits for each wing outline. A craft built for hypersonic speed must also fly at slow speeds. Its wing choice shapes balance in both regimes at once. Small outline changes can shift lift and upset trim. This study gave designers a fair test of rival wing plans for the flat-top craft then on drawing boards.
nasa-tm-19650019839-wing-sweep-and-blunt:
Robert D Witcofski and Don C Marcum Jr, aerospace engineers at Langley, studied delta wing shapes at Mach twenty, twenty times the speed of sound. Tests ran in helium tunnels, which can reach such extreme speeds. Their subject was how wing sweep and leading edge blunting change a delta planform's behavior at that speed.

At Mach twenty, a vehicle is in the hypersonic range of reentry flight. Small shape choices have large effects on lift, drag, and heating. The paper sets out the terms and measures used, then reports the effects found. Designers of very fast vehicles used such tunnel results to choose wing shapes with more confidence.
nasa-tm-19650024638-a-computer-program-t: A computer program to improve scheduling for STADAN, the space tracking and data acquisition network, is identified here by its July 1965 Goddard cover page alone. The hosted sample preserves only that cover and a general disclaimer, with no readable body text, author line, or program details. No further facts about the program can be grounded from the sample.
nasa-tm-19660014185-welding-procedures-f:
J J Vagi, R E Monroe, R M Evans, and D C Martin wrote this October 1965 guide to welding titanium and its alloys. It was prepared under the Redstone Scientific Information Center for the Army Missile Command. Welding titanium is tricky, because hot titanium soaks up gases from air and turns brittle. Their guide covers choosing conditions, equipment, and shop methods for sound joints.

A good titanium weld needs strict shielding from air until it cools. Small lapses make a joint that looks fine but cracks in service. Compiled procedures let shops repeat proven practice every time. For missile and aircraft work, where titanium carried growing loads, such a guide was a working necessity.
nasa-tm-19670009441-dual-frequency-20-0-:
Chesley H. Looney Jr., of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, compiled this data report in January 1967. It presents a year of very low frequency radio measurements at two close frequencies, 20.0 and 19.9 kilohertz. Such signals travel inside the ionosphere, so their timing shifts carry information about conditions overhead, including effects tied to solar activity.

Both signals came from station WWVL, each locked to the National Bureau of Standards master clock within a microsecond. Goddard received them with Tracor receivers referenced to a cesium-beam frequency standard, itself checked against hydrogen masers. Twelve tables give daily phase angle measurements, corrected using bureau data. The dual-frequency record, Looney explains, resolves a timing ambiguity inherent in the single 20.0 kilohertz signal, pinning the transmitted phase difference down tightly.
nasa-tm-19670024651-survey-of-the-region:
George Cope, of Woodstock College in Maryland, and Jaylee Burley, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, surveyed a star field. Their paper is dated February 1967. Their target is the region of I Lacerta, a star association in the constellation Lacerta. Star surveys count and classify the members of such groupings to map their extent and makeup.

The observations rest heavily on photographic plates, including Palomar plates whose locations are charted. An astrophotometer, whose optics are diagrammed, measured star brightnesses from the plates. Spectral classifications were transferred from special images and checked carefully. Two independent observers classified the same stars. The team's types were then compared with published classifications. Photometric calibration used stars of known spectral type. The results sections present star counts for the surveyed areas and the distribution of stars by spectral type.
nasa-tm-19680002484-nimbus-1-high-resolu:
Staff of the Laboratory for Atmospheric and Biological Science at Goddard Space Flight Center produced this data catalog in July 1966. It is Volume 2 of the Nimbus I high resolution radiation data catalog and user's manual. The volume covers the Nimbus Meteorological Radiation Tapes, called HRIR tapes.

Volume 1 had documented the same data as photo film strips. This volume documents the data after reduction for digital computers. The foreword credits the engineers who built the special digitizing equipment. It also credits those who wrote the processing programs and prepared the tapes. Weather researchers used the tapes to work with infrared pictures from orbit.
nasa-tm-19710004668-apollo-saturn-5-cons:
The Kennedy Space Center issued this consolidated instrumentation plan for AS-509, the Apollo 14 vehicle. D. E. Clark, chief of the Data Systems Division, originated the plan. It pulls the flight's measurement setup into one governing document.

A Saturn 5 flight carried hundreds of sensors for pressure, temperature, and vibration. The plan states which instruments fly, where they sit, and how their data flows. It opens with a list of effective pages, so every user can check that their copy is current. Flight teams and ground crews worked from the same pages. That shared record kept the Apollo 14 data system whole.
nasa-tm-19720010767-apollo-14-lunar-phot:
A T Anderson and M A Niksch of the National Space Science Data Center prepared this data users' note in August 1971. It is part one of the Apollo 14 lunar photography package. Anderson was the center's acquisition scientist, and Niksch its technical editor. The note announces that Apollo 14 pictures are available for study. It also helps investigators pick the right photographs. Apollo 14 had landed in the Fra Mauro hills that February.

Background sections describe the mission's goals and camera equipment. They also rate the coverage and quality of the pictures returned. The note explains the photo formats the center could supply. Ordering procedures close the document. Limited free copies served approved scientific studies and college courses. The center sits at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland.
obiter-dicta:
Augustine Birrell titled his essays Obiter Dicta, a law term he defines up front. An obiter dictum, says an old judge, is a gratuitous opinion, an individual impertinence. Wise or foolish, right or wrong, it binds none, not even the lips that utter it. Birrell dates his preface to the American edition February 13, 1885.

That preface calls the book a very little one to introduce to so large a continent. Scribner proposed the edition, and Birrell found being read in America delightful. Contents treat Carlyle, the alleged obscurity of Browning's poetry, and truth hunting. Actors, a rogue's memoirs, the via media, and Falstaff complete the list.
on-limitations-to-the-use-of-some-anthro:
John Wesley Powell wrote this paper for the Smithsonian Institution. Powell directed the Bureau of Ethnology at that time. He warns that archaeology findings are often misused. Workers had linked American tribes to ancient Old World races. Powell calls such uses of the data illegitimate.

He reviews mounds, graves, ruins, and scattered works of art. Such finds can show how art grew in early life, he says. They may hint at customs of their makers. But they cannot prove grand racial links abroad. He notes man's wide spread by very early times. The paper urges care and limits in science.
overland-through-asia-pictures-of-siberi:
Thomas Wallace Knox traveled overland through Asia in the 1860s. He published his Pictures of Siberian, Chinese, and Tartar Life at Hartford in 1871. Agents sold it by subscription only. Nearly two hundred illustrations and a map fill it. The full title promises travels in Kamchatka, Siberia, China, and Mongolia. Full accounts of the Siberian exiles come with them. Their treatment, condition, and mode of life are all described. The Amoor River and the frozen ocean's shores close the promise.

His preface notes that in fourteen years only one other book, Major Collins's Voyage Down the Amoor, had covered the ground. Knox crossed the Russian empire when the route was sleigh, boat, and horse. His sketches of exile colonies and river peoples made the book a standard American account of Siberia.
podcast-joerogan-J3Wqw8Az7TA:
Author Gregg Braden joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2387. Braden writes and lectures on human potential, arguing that people carry abilities that modern life teaches them to ignore. His books blend science claims with spiritual teaching, and they have found a large audience.

He lays out his case for Rogan: that the heart, the body, and old traditions hold knowledge science is only now measuring. Rogan asks where the proof is strong and where it is faith. The episode gives Braden's worldview a full, friendly hearing, and listeners can judge how much of it they buy.
podcast-joerogan-wf0_nMaQ6tA:
Eric Weinstein sits with Joe Rogan for episode 1453, an early long talk before his own show made him famous. Weinstein, a mathematician and economist, had been promoting his Geometric Unity theory of physics for years. Mainstream physics had largely ignored it, and that snub shapes the talk.

Weinstein explains why he thinks academia punishes bold ideas and protects its gatekeepers. He outlines his theory in broad strokes and the cold shoulder it received. Rogan asks how a smart outsider should judge such claims. Theory fans get a window into a feud between one mind and a whole field.
sacred-books-east-vol-10-dhammapada-sutt:
Volume ten of the Sacred Books of the East, issued in 1881, joins two of the oldest Buddhist texts: the Dhammapada and the Sutta-Nipata. F. Max Müller translated both from the Pali. Müller edited the whole Sacred Books series at Oxford, which carried Asia's scriptures to English readers.

The Dhammapada holds 423 short verses on the mind, anger, craving, and the path to release. Its lines are the best-known words of Buddhism in the West. The Sutta-Nipata is older and rawer: poems of wandering monks, snakes, and fierce self-reliance. Together they give the Buddha's teaching in its most direct, quotable form.
selections-from-previous-works-with-rema:
Samuel Butler issued this gathering of his earlier pieces with Trubner in London in 1884. Alongside the chosen pieces stand remarks on G. J. Romanes and his book on mind growth in animals, plus Butler's comic poem A Psalm of Montreal. A sharp preface opens the quarrel.

Butler charges that Romanes cited a Canon Kingsley piece on instinct from a journal that did not yet exist at the date given. He notes that he asked in print for the true source and got no answer. Wit and grievance mix here, as Butler defends his own views on memory passed from parent to young.
seraphita:
Honore de Balzac wrote this mystical tale, here in English by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. Balzac inscribed the work to Madame Eveline de Hanska, who had asked him for it. He calls it a sketch of a figure dreamed of since childhood, drawn from the depths of mystic thought.

The tale opens on the wild coast of Norway, beneath strange northern skies. A being named Seraphitus stands at its heart, loved and wondered at by those nearby. Balzac blends love story with Swedenborg-style teaching on spirit and heaven. The book closes his studies of faith with a strange, glowing vision of the soul's ascent.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States built from talks with former slaves, was typed from records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together at Washington in 1941. One part is Volume II, the Arkansas Narratives, Part I. Its list of those who spoke begins with Silas Abbott, Lucian Abernathy, Laura Adeline, Aunt Adway, Rose Aiken, and Liddie Aldridge.
texas-a-brief-account-of-the-origin-prog:
Texas, a brief account of the rise and state of the colonial settlements of Texas, came out in 1836 as a short pamphlet pulled from a larger work then near press. Some parts had run first in the New Orleans Bee and Bulletin.

Its preface warns that war fills the day, so only a slice of the source work's public case is given here. The writer argues that Texas settlers were forced into war with Mexico by steady abuse and breach of rights. Their fight, he says, seeks freedom and sound rule, not gain or conquest. Readers get a wartime plea for the Texas cause, made in the year of the revolt itself.
the-great-north-western-conspiracy-in-al:
I. Winslow Ayer wrote The Great North-Western Conspiracy in All Its Startling Details. Ayer was a doctor of medicine. His long title page lists the matter: the plot to plunder and burn Chicago, free rebel prisoners, and seize arsenals. It promises raids from Canada, a plot to burn New York, and piracy on the Lakes. Portraits of leading characters go with the text.

His introduction takes up the trial before the Military Commission in Cincinnati. That trial, he says, drew out testimony of the most startling kind. It showed a deep, well-arranged conspiracy, favored in the great cities of six states. But for timely discovery, he argues, it would have ended in disaster. He credits a merciful Providence for the country's escape. The book is his full account of the plot and its trial.
the-inca-of-perusalem-an-almost-historic:
George Bernard Shaw called this wartime playlet an almost historical comedietta. His preface insists on when he wrote it. The central figure was still a feared foe then. The Caesar of the piece was no fallen prisoner. Many readers could not forgive Shaw's laughter. Laughing at a deadly peril seemed heartless. Anyone doubting German skill in war risked a hard name. Such doubters were called pro-German.

The fighting has since shown the Inca was doomed. Shaw now faces the opposite charge. Critics may say he hits a man when he is down. He reports cutting any foul blows from the proofs. The play first reached an English stage in 1917. The Pioneer Players performed it at the Criterion Theatre. Its prologue opens with an English archdeacon. He comes through the curtains in extreme irritation.
the-jew-of-malta: Marlowe's fierce 1590 tragedy about Barabas, the rich Jew of Malta, who answers Christian persecution with spectacular revenge. Bloody, blackly comic, and deliberately shocking, it gave the Elizabethan stage one of its great villains. The play's portrait of greed and hatred still provokes, and its verse still thunders.
the-life-of-the-truly-eminent-and-learne:
M. de Burigny wrote his life of Hugo Grotius in French, and this English edition appeared in London in 1754. His preface wishes that so celebrated a genius had found a historian equal to his fame. Earlier writers, he says, gave only surface accounts of the life plus catalogues of the works.

Burigny promises a full history of Grotius important negotiations and a critical account of his writings. He praises Lehman defense of Grotius memory as fuller than the rest. Charles Butler later life of Grotius, held elsewhere in this library, drew heavily on Burigny work.
the-magna-carta:
Magna Carta itself, the great charter of 1215, is the text held here, in a file whose preparer's note admits that some versions arrived a little mangled in transit. The charter opens in King John's own voice. John, by the grace of God King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and Count of Anjou, greets his archbishops and bishops. Abbots, earls, barons, and officials are greeted too. John states that the grant is made for the health of his soul and his ancestors' and heirs'.

He acts on the advice of named churchmen and barons, from Archbishop Stephen of Canterbury to William Marshal, Earl of Pembroke. Its first clause grants that the English Church shall be free, with its rights undiminished, for the king and his heirs in perpetuity. Readers meet the famous document directly, in its own formal language.
the-mansion-of-mystery-being-a-certain-c:
Chester K. Steele's The Mansion of Mystery, published in 1911 by the International Fiction Library, presents itself as a case taken from the note-book of Adam Adams, investigator and detective. Chapter one, The Story of a Double Tragedy, opens with a young man in a tremendous hurry. First ashore from the ferryboat, he leaps into a taxicab and orders the driver to take him to the Vanderslip Building with all possible speed.

In the cab he buries his chin in his hands. His handsome face is wrinkled with care, his hair disheveled, and he looks as if he has lost much sleep. "To think that she is guilty!" he mutters, shaking as if with fever, and twice starts up to check whether he has arrived. Steele opens his detective tale on a client's anguish before the investigator even appears.
the-naturalist-in-la-plata:
W. H. Hudson's The Naturalist in La Plata, in a third edition published in New York by D. Appleton and Company in 1895, carries illustrations by J. Smit. Hudson, joint author of Argentine Ornithology, explains his plan in a preface. He sifted and arranged facts about the habits of the animals he knew best, keeping only what seemed worth recording, and grouped linked subjects under single headings.

Much of the material first appeared as papers in the Field and other natural history journals, and in magazines such as Longman's and The Nineteenth Century, whose editors allowed reuse. Hudson apologises for an unoriginal title in the line of The Naturalist on the Amazons. Birds, he notes, gave him most pleasure, though most of his fresh bird knowledge sits in his earlier book.
the-outdoor-girls-on-pine-island-or-a-ca: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls on Pine Island, or A Cave and What It Contained, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The lists show Pine Island as the seventh Outdoor Girls volume, after Ocean View. Hope's Moving Picture Girls series, from Oak Farm to At Sea, and her Bobbsey Twins books fill the remaining space, at 50 cents a volume.
the-story-of-malta: Maturin M. Ballou's history of Malta, dated 1893, is presented here through its opening publisher's pages alone. Those pages list Ballou's other travel books. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published them. Equatorial America and Aztec Land stand among them. A summer journey to Alaska follows. Volumes of travels due west, south, and north come next. Then the title page of the Malta volume begins. Ballou's account of the island itself does not appear.
the-suppression-of-the-african-slave-tra: Volume one of a Harvard Historical Studies monograph appeared in 1896. Longmans, Green, and Company published it. It treats the suppression of the African slave-trade to the United States, 1638 to 1870. No author's name is printed here. Only the title page and a detailed contents opening appear here. An introductory chapter gives the plan of the work and the rise of the English slave-trade. Chapters on restrictions follow. They treat the planting colonies of Georgia and the Carolinas. Virginia and Maryland come next. The history itself does not appear.
the-uttermost-farthing-a-savant-s-vendet:
R. Austin Freeman subtitles his Uttermost Farthing A Savant's Vendetta, sharing a title and motto idea with a very different novel. The narrator publishes, with misgivings, the strange history confided by his late friend Humphrey Challoner. Challoner's ethical standards, he warns, stand far from ordinary ones and may repel readers.

Challoner was a great savant spoiled by untimely wealth, once noted as a comparative anatomist and criminal anthropologist. When known to the narrator he seemed a mere collector, endlessly adding specimens to a private museum. Later revelations changed that picture. Contents chapters promise a motive force, numbered victims, gifts of chance, and a serpent's trail, marking the story as methodical revenge.
the-valley-of-vision-a-book-of-romance-a:
Henry Van Dyke calls The Valley of Vision a book of romance and some half-told tales, dedicating it to his children and grandchildren. His preface answers a friend who asked why a valley, not a mountaintop, should give the widest view. Van Dyke replies that the mountaintop overlooks earth and sea, but the deepest visions of life's meaning come in valleys.

Suffering, endurance, and self-sacrifice are the valley's teachers in his account. He reads the recent world war as a victory over Germany's peak-born illusion of world dominion, won by Allied strength grown through valley visions of right and justice. The tales themselves are fables and fantasies, sketches grave and gay, where more is meant than meets the ear.
un-doc-declaration-of-alma-ata:
The Declaration of Alma-Ata came out of the International Conference on Primary Health Care. World Health Organization and UNICEF backing brought the meeting to Alma-Ata in September 1978. Health gaps between rich and poor lands were wide and growing. The delegates sought a fairer base for care.

Health, the text says, is full physical, mental, and social well-being. It is a basic human right, not a prize for the few. The goal set was health for all by the year 2000. Basic care near home is the key: clean water, food, shots, mother and child care, and vital drugs. Local people must help plan and run that care.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Specific Problems with Personal Data forms part of the United Nations manual on computer crime, printed in the International Review of Criminal Policy, Nos. 43 and 44. Police work now means gathering and linking files on named people. That power sits uneasily next to privacy. Each land draws the line in a different place.

The survey points to one landmark court ruling. West Germany's top court held that state storage of personal facts can chill free action. A clear law must back each such file, the court said. Some newer state charters name data privacy outright. In most lands, though, the rules sit in mixed spots: trial codes, data acts, or police laws. Hard limits on police files stay rare.
vendetta:
Honore de Balzac wrote Vendetta, rendered into English by Katharine Prescott Wormeley. He dedicated it to Puttinati, a sculptor of Milan. Chapter one, a prologue, opens in the year 1800, late in October. The scene stands before the palace of the Tuileries in Paris. A foreigner waits for a long time near a house just pulled down. A woman and a little girl wait with him.

The man folds his arms and bows his head. Then he lifts it, to look from the palace to his wife. She plays with the child's long black hair, yet misses none of his glances. Balzac says some bond other than love ties them, and names it: misery. Misery, he adds, is perhaps the strongest of all ties. The stranger's broad head and black hair streaked with white mark a proud Corsican exile. The tale builds toward the feud of its title.
woodroffe-shakti-and-shakta:
John Woodroffe, a Calcutta judge, wrote Shakti and Shakta in 1918 as Arthur Avalon. His book gives the classic English account of Tantric Shaktism. The worship of the Divine Mother stands at its warm center.

Woodroffe treats the Goddess as the world's living power and soul. He explains her rites, mantras, and images with a scholar's care. His sympathy for a faith mocked by many set the work apart. Western readers met Tantra as deep thought, not mere scandal, here. The book launched the modern study of Tantra in English for good. Its chapters still serve as the first door into Shakta thought.
